turns.narration:
**Chapter 2: Four Days**

The fog sat on the Rhoyne like wet wool, and the camp woke coughing into it.

Marro was up before the drums. He always was now. The splinted fingers throbbed when the cold got into them, and the cold had got into everything. He worked the whetstone along the cudgel's iron band for something to do with his good hand. You couldn't sharpen a cudgel. He did it anyway.

Four days to the new moon. Thirty stags. He had four. The arithmetic didn't improve with looking.

Hesse came down the picket line leading Ash, who walked like an old man on a bad stair. The patch over her left eye was dark with damp. She stopped beside him and watched the wall, not him.

"They doubled the torches on the Black Wall last night," she said. "Counted them from the ditch. Forty where there were twenty."

"Maybe they're cold too."

"Maybe." She scratched Ash under the jaw. "The grain barges didn't come either. Triarch's credit, Triarch's barges. Funny thing, a creditor going shy."

Across the mud, the flap of Rickard's tent opened. The captain came out with his left arm strapped to his chest and his face grey under the burn scar. He looked older than he had a week ago. He saw Marro and lifted his chin: *come here.*

Marro went.

Inside, the tent smelled of tallow and old blood. A strongbox sat at the foot of the cot. Rickard eased himself onto a stool and didn't sit down so much as stop falling.

"I need someone across the river," he said. "Into the east city. Quiet. A message to a man in the Dragon's Den, and an answer back before nightfall." He looked at Marro's hand, then his face. "Bridge is shut. You'll have to find another way over. Can you do it?"

The Dragon's Den. Lissa's mother lived there. The letter sat folded against Marro's ribs, under the borrowed cloak.

Outside, Hesse had stopped walking Ash. She stood just past the tent flap, close enough to hear.

turns.player: I stand behind Rickard at the captains' council in the big pavilion, holding his helm.
turns.narration:
The big pavilion stank of wet canvas and too many men who'd slept in their mail.

Marro stood behind Rickard's stool with the helm in both hands, the good one doing the work, the splinted fingers just resting on the crest. Rickard sat with his left arm bound against his chest. He hadn't tried to hide it. Nobody in the pavilion was fool enough to mention it either.

The captains took the benches along the table. At the head, Lysono Qhoran had his ledgers open and his sleeves pinned back so the ink wouldn't touch them. He didn't look up when he spoke.

"Two months of grain on the Triarch's credit," he said. "The barges that were to bring the third did not come this morning. And last night, the wall doubled its torches." Now he looked up. "I would like to know how the Triarch knows when to be careful, when we have told him nothing."

Nobody answered. Somebody's bench creaked.

"Someone talks," Lysono said, mild as milk. "I keep the books. I will find the line that doesn't add."

Rickard said nothing. His jaw worked once under the burn scar, and then he was still. Marro watched the back of his neck, where the cord of the strongbox key disappeared under his collar, and couldn't have said why he was watching it.

At the far end of the table, Ser Tobbin pushed himself up. Big man, rust on his gorget, eyes red like he'd been drinking or not sleeping.

"While we're counting," he said, "count my sister. Dagna. She was to meet me three nights back with a boat and she never came." He swept the table with a look and stopped on Marro. "You were in the alleys by the river that night, squire. Half the camp saw you come back with your hand broke. You see her?"

The pavilion went quiet in the way rooms do when everyone has decided to listen without seeming to.

The helm was suddenly very heavy. Marro could feel the river cold again, the weight going over the edge, the splash that wasn't loud enough.

Rickard didn't turn around. Hesse, by the tent pole, shifted her one eye to Marro and kept it there.

turns.player: A captain asks why the Triarch would feed an army camped outside his own walls. I keep quiet and watch Rickard's face.
turns.narration:
Marro said nothing. Tobbin waited for it, then didn't, and his mouth went flat.

Before he could push, a grey-bearded captain on the near bench slapped the table. "Leave the boy. Here's the thing I want answered." He jabbed a finger toward the wall none of them could see through the canvas. "Why does a Triarch feed an army sitting in his ditch? You don't sell bread to the man who's come to burn your house. Not unless you know he won't."

That landed. Benches creaked. Somebody laughed and stopped.

Marro watched Rickard.

Wits check: (1+4) +2 Wits = 7.

The captain's face didn't move. That was the first thing. Rickard had a good face for councils, all scar and patience. But his right hand had come up off his knee, slow, like a man brushing at a fly, and settled at his collar. On the cord. Thumb on the cord, through the cloth, where the key hung. He held it there for the space of a breath and then let the hand fall, easy, and said, "Because a Triarch thinks further than a ditch. He wants us hungry and grateful, not gone. Credit's a leash."

It was a decent answer. Two captains nodded.

Marro's stomach had gone cold and tight anyway. He'd seen that hand before, on other men, at the dice table, when they had a bad throw under the cup and were praying nobody lifted it.

He looked away too late.

Lysono Qhoran was watching him. Not Rickard. Him. The paymaster's pen had stopped over the ledger, and his eyes went from Marro's face to Rickard's collar and back, and then he dipped the pen and wrote something short.

"Credit is a leash," Lysono agreed pleasantly. "And leashes have two ends."

Down the table, Tobbin was still standing. "I asked the squire a question," he said.

turns.player: Someone says the Triarch seems to know our plans before we make them. The captains turn to Rickard.
turns.narration:
"He knows them before we've made them," said a younger captain with a Lysene braid. "The ford at the south bend, a fortnight back. They were waiting with pitch. We'd decided it that same night, in this tent."

Then they were all looking at Rickard. Not accusing. Not yet. Just looking at the man whose plans they were.

Rickard let them. He took his time about it, the way he did with a horse that wanted to bolt, and when he spoke his voice was flat and tired and reasonable.

"Then there's a mouth in this camp," he said. "Could be a cook. Could be a whore who hears a captain brag. Could be one of you." He let that sit. "So the next plan doesn't come to this table. I'll draw it and hold it, and you'll get your orders the morning you march and not an hour before."

Grumbling, but the grumbling of men who'd heard worse ideas.

"Hold it yourself," Lysono said, not looking up from his ledger. "In the strongbox, I imagine. Very safe." The pen scratched. "I will want to see it, captain. The company pays for these plans. The company reads them."

"When they're done."

"Of course."

Marro had the helm against his chest now, both arms around it like a shield he wasn't allowed to carry. He could feel the shape of the thing in the room, the way you feel a step in the dark before your foot finds it. He didn't have a name for it. He didn't want one.

Ser Tobbin hadn't sat down. He'd waited out the whole exchange with his fists on the table and his red eyes on Marro, and now the talk had moved on without him, which only made it worse.

"Squire," he said again, quieter. "My sister."

Hesse straightened off the tent pole.

turns.player: Rickard calls for his shield and says he will lead the first assault himself. I step forward to hand it to him.
turns.narration:
"Shield," Rickard said, before Tobbin could say the name again. "The first assault, I lead it myself. Let the wall see whose plan it is."

It cut the room clean in half. Half the captains thumped the table. Tobbin's mouth closed on whatever he'd been about to say.

Marro set the helm down on the stool's end and fetched the shield from where it leaned by the tent pole. Oak and iron, the company's black skulls on gold gone dull with river damp. Heavy enough that his splinted hand complained just lifting the edge. He stepped up and held it out to Rickard's left side, the way he'd done a hundred mornings.

Rickard's left arm didn't move.

It couldn't. It sat bound against his chest where the bolt had gone in, and the strap that should have taken the shield's weight hung there with nothing to take. For a moment the two of them stood like that, the squire holding out the shield and the captain looking at it, and the whole pavilion saw it.

Then Rickard reached across with his right hand, took the shield by its rim, and set it down against his own knee. "When the arm's healed," he said, pleasant, as if he'd meant to do exactly that.

Nobody thumped the table now.

"When," said Lysono Qhoran, and wrote.

The grey-bearded captain cleared his throat and said the assault could wait for the plan in any case, and that was the end of it. The benches emptied in twos and threes. Tobbin went out last but one, and at the flap he turned and found Marro across the trampled rushes.

"Tonight," he said. "You and me. We'll talk about the river."

He let the canvas fall behind him.

Rickard sat with the shield against his knee and didn't look at anyone. His thumb had found the cord at his collar again.

Hesse came off her tent pole and stood beside Marro, close, her one eye on the flap where Tobbin had gone. "You've got the day," she said, low. "Rickard's errand, or Tobbin's talk, or Pallo's grey men. You won't get all three."

(OOC) Done. The council scene is closed and logged: the missing barges, the ambush at the south-bend ford, Rickard keeping the next plan to himself and failing to take his shield in front of the captains, Lysono watching you watch Rickard, and Ser Tobbin wanting a word about the river tonight. New open threads are "Tobbin's question" and "Rickard's errand", alongside Pallo's debt (due in four days) and Lissa's letter.

When you're ready, tell me where Marro goes next.
